title: Chapter 5 — Breakfast
paragraphs: I quickly followed suit and went down to the bar room, greeting the grinning landlord pleasantly enough. I bore him no grudge, despite his pranks regarding my bedfellow.

A good laugh is a mighty good thing, and too rare in this world. So if any person naturally provides material for a good joke, they shouldn't hold back — let them cheerfully spend themselves that way. And anyone who has something genuinely laughable about them, you can be sure there's more to them than meets the eye.

The bar room was now full of boarders who'd been arriving the night before, and whom I hadn't yet gotten a good look at. They were nearly all whalemen — chief mates, second mates, third mates, ship carpenters, coopers, blacksmiths, harpooneers, and ship keepers. A brown, brawny company with bushy beards — an unshaven, shaggy bunch, all wearing their monkey jackets as morning robes.

You could easily tell how long each one had been ashore. This young fellow's ruddy cheek was the color of a sun-ripened pear and seemed to smell just as sweet — he couldn't have been off his ship more than three days. The man next to him was a few shades lighter — a touch of satinwood in his complexion. A third still showed a tropical tan, though slightly faded — he'd probably been ashore for weeks. But who could match Queequeg's cheek? Striped with various shades, it looked like the western slope of the Andes, displaying a whole array of contrasting climates, zone by zone.
'Grub, ho!' cried the landlord, throwing open a door, and in we went to breakfast.

They say that men who've seen the world become perfectly at ease in any company. Not always, though. Ledyard, the great New England traveler, and Mungo Park, the Scottish one — of all men, they had the least social confidence. But perhaps crossing Siberia in a dog sled, or taking a long solitary walk on an empty stomach through the heart of Africa, may not be the best training for polite society. Still, that kind of worldly awkwardness can be found anywhere.

These reflections occurred to me because after we were all seated at the table, and I was expecting to hear some good whaling stories, nearly everyone maintained a profound silence. And not only that — they looked embarrassed. Here were sea dogs, many of whom had boarded great whales on the open ocean without flinching — complete strangers to them — and fought them to the death without blinking. Yet here they sat at a social breakfast table, all in the same profession, all sharing the same interests, looking around as sheepishly as if they'd never left some mountain farm. A strange sight — these bashful bears, these timid warrior whalemen!

But Queequeg sat among them — at the head of the table, as it happened — cool as an icicle. I can't say much for his table manners. His greatest admirer couldn't have justified his bringing the harpoon to breakfast and using it without ceremony — reaching across the table with it, endangering many heads, and spearing beefsteaks toward himself. But he did it so coolly, and everyone knows that in most people's estimation, doing anything coolly is doing it with style.

We won't dwell on all of Queequeg's peculiarities here — how he avoided coffee and hot rolls and devoted his full attention to beefsteaks, done rare. Enough to say that after breakfast he withdrew like the others to the public room, lit his tomahawk-pipe, and sat there quietly digesting and smoking with his inseparable hat on, while I headed out for a walk.
